opus-5.5.text:
So when I think about library learning, I think about how mathematics actually grows as a human discipline. Mathematicians don't prove every theorem from the axioms. We build up a library of definitions, lemmas, and abstractions, and then we reuse them. A huge part of being a good mathematician is knowing which concepts to invent. Think about a group, a sheaf, or a spectral sequence. Each one compresses an enormous amount of reasoning into one reusable object.

For AI, that's the hard part. Current systems, including the ones doing really well on competition problems, are mostly solving one problem at a time. They search for a proof, maybe in Lean, and once they find it the episode is basically over. What they don't do well is look back across thousands of proofs and say, "this pattern keeps showing up, let me name it, state it as a general lemma, prove it once, and add it to my toolbox so future proofs get shorter."

So the challenge has a few layers. The first is discovery: finding abstractions that are actually useful, not just syntactic coincidences. The second is generality: the lemma has to be stated at the right level. If it's too specific it's useless, and if it's too general it may be false or hard to prove. The third is maintenance. Libraries like Mathlib are living things. Definitions get refactored, naming conventions matter, and a new concept has to fit coherently with everything already there. The last is evaluation. How do you reward a model for inventing a good definition, when the payoff only shows up much later, across many downstream problems? That's a very sparse, long-horizon credit assignment problem.

That's why I see library learning as close to the heart of what it would mean for AI to do research mathematics rather than solve problems. Competition math tests whether you can use known tools cleverly. Research math is very often about building the right tools. If we want AI that can contribute something like a new theory, and not just a new proof, it has to learn to grow and curate its own library, ideally in collaboration with the human community that maintains these formal libraries.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI inventing useful concepts and lemmas, but does not ask whether an AI that can make mathematical conjectures can also formulate definitions.

r002.rationale: It describes building a reusable library of definitions and proved lemmas, then drawing on patterns across proofs to add new concepts and results for future work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think library learning is actually one of the most underappreciated bottlenecks in getting AI to do real mathematics, so I'm glad you're asking about it.

Here's the way I think about it. When a human mathematician works on a problem, they're not starting from axioms every time. They're standing on an enormous accumulated library: definitions, lemmas, techniques, and a kind of tacit sense of which tools tend to be useful in which situations. That library isn't static. Every time you prove something, you potentially add to it. A good mathematician is constantly noticing, "oh, this argument I just did is actually a general pattern, let me abstract it," and then that abstraction becomes a reusable building block.

Most current AI systems don't really do that. They either operate from a fixed context, where you give them a problem and they attack it fresh, or they rely on whatever happened to be in pretraining. Even in formal settings like Lean, where you have Mathlib as a literal library, the model is mostly a consumer of the library rather than a contributor to it. It searches for existing lemmas, it doesn't write new ones that it then uses in the next problem.

So the challenge is really threefold. First, abstraction: can the system recognize when a piece of reasoning it just did is worth generalizing and storing? That's hard because you don't want to store everything, you'd drown in noise. Second, retrieval: once you've built a library of thousands of learned concepts, can you find the right one when it's relevant? That's not just keyword matching, it's a judgment call about structural similarity. And third, composition: can you actually combine those learned pieces into something new, rather than just pattern-matching to a single lemma?

What makes this exciting to me is that it's where the research-math question and the AI question really converge. In competition math, you can kind of get away without a growing library, because the space of techniques is bounded. In research math, the whole game is building new tools. The person who proves a hard theorem usually does it by inventing a concept nobody had before, and then that concept lives on. If we want AI to contribute to mathematics in a lasting way, it has to participate in that cycle of building, storing, and reusing. Otherwise it's just solving isolated puzzles.

There's also a very practical side. Formal libraries like Mathlib are built by humans at enormous effort. If a model could learn to extend the library itself, verified by the proof assistant so you know it's correct, that compounds. Every solved problem makes the next one easier. That's the flywheel I think we should be aiming for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning and extending a mathematical library, but does not ask whether an AI that makes conjectures can also formulate definitions.

r002.rationale: It describes proofs being abstracted into reusable library building blocks, then stored and reused to build further results, presenting library growth as an ongoing cycle.

astra-6.text:
I think of library learning as the challenge of discovering reusable structure. In mathematics, when we solve a problem, we don’t just want to keep that particular solution. We want to ask: Is there a useful lemma here? Is there a definition that makes the argument clearer? Can this technique help us solve a whole family of problems?

For an AI system, that means going beyond proving theorems within a fixed library. It also needs to learn what to add to the library. And that’s a difficult judgment: something too specific may never be useful again, while something too general may be difficult to apply or expensive to prove.

There’s also a connection between building the library and searching it. A new abstraction can make future proofs much shorter, but adding thousands of unhelpful lemmas can make finding the right one harder. So the challenge is to develop a body of mathematical knowledge that actually improves the system’s ability to reason. That seems like an important part of moving from solving isolated problems to doing mathematics cumulatively.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether definitions are useful and says an AI should learn what to add to a library, but it does not ask whether an AI that makes mathematical conjectures can also formulate definitions.

r002.rationale: The response describes building a useful library and moving toward cumulative mathematics, but does not clearly describe iterative theory construction based on existing definitions and proved results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of library learning as the challenge of discovering reusable mathematical building blocks. When we solve a problem, we don’t want to keep only the final proof. We also want to ask: Was there a useful intermediate lemma, a definition, or a technique that could help us solve other problems?

That creates an interesting challenge for AI, because adding everything to a library isn’t necessarily helpful. You need to decide which abstractions are worth keeping, how to organize them, and when to retrieve them. A lemma might make one proof shorter but be too specific to help anywhere else.

So the goal is a system whose experience changes the way it approaches future problems. It solves problems, extracts useful structure, and builds a library that makes subsequent reasoning more effective. That feedback loop seems like an important part of moving from solving individual mathematical problems to developing mathematical knowledge.
